title: Taser not connected to death of North Bay man in 2018
article: Evidence presented today points to other causes related to the death Gordon Dale Couvrette after incident with police
A development came on day three of the inquest into the death of Gordon Dale Couvrette on Feb. 22, 2018.

Initially it was stated that Couvrette died after being Tasered by a North Bay police officer, however evidence was given that the North Bay resident may not have died because of the Taser, but perhaps from a condition described as Excited Delirium. Taking the stand for a second straight day, North Bay Police Constable Steve Sproule responded to a new report that indicated 'no connection' was made by the Conducted Ener gy Weapon (Taser) when used on Couvrette during the struggle. Sproule, an expert on CEW usage, said that looking at the data that there was 'no connection made' by the Taser in this incident, meaning there is no way to confirm Couvrette was struck by the charge a Taser emits. Dr. Martin Queen, who performed an autopsy on Couvrette also testified Wednesday.

Dr. Queen is a forensic pathologist employed at Health Sciences North in Sudbury . Dr Queen told the Inquest he has performed more than seven thousand autopsies in his career and 350 homicide - related postmortems . The forensic pathologist stated that the fact that the Taser had 'no connection' made the case that t his weapon did not fact or in Couvrette's death.

Dr. Queen says the likely cause of the death , in a separate report compiled by a toxicologist, was the combination of cocaine , m eth amphetamine and traces of drug by-products in Couvrette's system combined with a struggle with the po lic e .
Couvrette died of cardiac arrest as police and first responders could not revive him.

Queen also contended that the police's action of restraint did not kill Couvrette from what he could ascertain . The forensic pathologist said that asphyxia could have played a role in the man's death , but again, there was nothing definitive.
There was much discussion about Couvrette being in a state of Excited Delirium .

Excited Delirium is described as an acute confusional state marked by intense paranoia, hallucinations, and violence toward objects and people. The most common causes seen today are toxicity from stimulant drugs, especially cocaine and methamphetamine, and psychiatric patients who stop taking their medication. Dr. Queen said the report he received about the incident suggested that Couvrette exhibited 'almost all' of the symptoms connected to this state.
Later in the day the Inquest heard testimony from Dr. Gillian Elizabeth Scott Munro .
Dr. Munro is a psychiatrist at the North Bay Regional Health Centre . She was tasked with examining data connected to this case.
Dr. Munro says that the medical community has very differing opinions on the existence of Excited Delirium.
Dr Munro talked about a condition called Autonomic Hypertension Syndrome .
Dr. Munro revealed that Couvrette had been diagnosed with Bi-Polar 1 disorder. A s ymptom of this disorder is manic episodes.
Dr. Munro hopes that in the future first responders receive training to recognize these symptoms although she admits that it is difficult when a snap decision is needed.
Dr. Munro would not say this type of training could have prevented Couvrette's death, but it may prevent one in the future.
An inquest into his death is mandatory under the Coroners Act . The S pecial I nv estigations Unit cleared police of any wrongdoing.
The goal of the inquest is to allow the jury to choose recommendations to prevent future deaths in similar circumstances. The Inquest continues at the Best Western at 9 a.m. on Thursday .
